title: Anthropic releases Opus 5.5 and cuts pricing by 20%. Your agent calls might secretly get routed to an older model.
excerpt: Anthropic released Claude Opus 5.5, cutting API pricing 20% (to $4/$20 per million input/output tokens) while claiming ~40% overall savings due to fewer tokens...
content_html:
Anthropic released Claude Opus 5.5, cutting API pricing 20% (to $4/$20 per million input/output tokens) while claiming ~40% overall savings due to fewer tokens needed and 30% faster output. It beats Fable 5.1 on several agentic coding benchmarks (Terminal-Bench, FrontierCode, CursorBench) at a fraction of the cost, and enterprise testers (Box, GitHub, Deloitte) reported fewer tokens and steps needed to complete tasks. A key architectural caveat: Anthropic's safety classifiers can silently reroute individual requests within a multi-turn agent workflow to older models (Opus 4.8 or Opus 5) rather than Opus 5.5, creating inconsistency that evals assuming a single model may miss. Opus 5.5 also posted the strongest internal alignment results to date, and Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 are expected soon.

Questions this post answers

How much does Claude Opus 5.5 cost compared to Opus 5?

Opus 5.5 costs $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, 20% less than Opus 5's $5 and $25. Cache reads drop to $0.20 from $0.50, and cache writes fall to $5 from $6.25. Anthropic estimates overall savings closer to 40% because Opus 5.5 uses fewer tokens per task and generates output over 30% faster. Teams comparing model costs for agentic coding can follow pricing shifts like this on daily.dev.

Can my Claude Opus 5.5 API requests get silently handled by a different, older model?

Yes. Anthropic's safety classifiers can reroute individual requests within a workflow to Opus 4.8 or Opus 5 instead of Opus 5.5, depending on whether safeguards intervene. In a multi-turn agent workflow this means different steps could be handled by models with different capabilities, an inconsistency that evals built on a single-model assumption may not catch. Developers architecting multi-step agent workflows track routing quirks like this on daily.dev.

How does Claude Opus 5.5 perform against GPT-6 Astra and GPT-5.6 Sol on coding benchmarks?

On FrontierCode at default effort, Opus 5.5 beats GPT-6 Astra at roughly 20% of the per-task cost. On CursorBench 4.0, it scores 57.8% versus GPT-5.6 Sol's 41.7%, at about a third of the cost. Opus 5.5 also scored 66.4% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 versus Fable 5.1's 55.8%. Engineers picking a model for agentic coding weigh benchmarks like these before committing on daily.dev.
